summary: DiDPO is a critic-free RL algorithm for training small coding models in a multi-turn add/delete edit loop. It splits each step's code diff into sub-diffs, aligns similar sub-diffs across rollouts of the same task via a 'groupability score', and adds a sub-diff-level group-relative advantage to the usual trajectory-level GRPO advantage. Evaluated on Qwen2.5-Coder-7B and Qwen3.5-4B over function-level and competitive-programming benchmarks, it beats GRPO, GiGPO and CodeRL+ by a few points; the authors also release a verl-code RL codebase.

claims.claim: DiDPO achieves the highest average across benchmarks: 48.4% (Qwen2.5-Coder-7B) and 58.6% (Qwen3.5-4B), beating GiGPO by 4.2 and 4.9 points.
claims.evidence: Table 1 and §5.2. Evaluation averaged over 5 sampled runs (App. E) but single training seed per method, no std reported.

claims.claim: On Qwen2.5-Coder-7B, DiDPO exceeds comparable methods by over 10%.
claims.evidence: Body reports +5.6 points over GRPO and +4.2 over GiGPO on average (≈13% and ≈9.5% relative); 'over 10%' only holds against GRPO in relative terms or on selected splits (e.g., +10.4 on APPS Interview).

claims.claim: Sub-diff credit is responsible for the gain over GRPO.
claims.evidence: Table 3 ablation on APPS/OJBench: full 31.3/8.0; w/o diff-level advantage 23.8/5.7; w/o sub-diff 25.0/4.4. Only one backbone, two benchmarks, no variance; lambda=1.2 selected by sensitivity curve without stated held-out tuning split.

claims.claim: DiDPO adds only ~2.3% training overhead over GRPO.

patterns.note: Fine-grained RL credit on code diffs improves small models on competitive programming; not shown for repository tasks.
Relies on test execution as the verifiable reward.

methodology.sample: Training on filtered PRIME data plus ~3K SFT cold-start trajectories (Qwen3.6-27B rollouts on GPT-5.5-augmented tasks); evaluation on APPS, HumanEval, MBPP, LiveCodeBench, LeetCode, USACO, OJBench, ICPC.
methodology.baselines: GRPO, GiGPO, CodeRL+ (same hyper-parameters), CoT/CodeAct/Self-Planning prompting, and large models (Kimi-K2.6, Qwen3.6-27B, GLM-5.2, GPT-5.5) as reference ceilings.
methodology.variance: Validation averaged over 5 sampled runs; no training seeds, std or CIs.
methodology.ablations: Groupability score design, component removal, lambda sensitivity, overhead.
methodology.contamination_controls: Training set filtered against validation set; LiveCodeBench cited as reduced-contamination; HumanEval/MBPP/APPS are public and likely in pretraining.
methodology.languages: Python competitive programming; edit actions restricted to add/delete in a temp dir.

standards.artifacts: verl-code codebase at github.com/xuc865/verl-code; trained checkpoints and SFT data release not stated.

biases.detail: 'Long-horizon coding agent' tasks are single-file algorithmic problems with add/delete actions, not repository work.
All benchmarks are Python code generation.
Single training run per method; 4-5 point margins without seeds.
'Over 10%' and 'principled framework' overstate a 4-6 point average gain.
HumanEval/MBPP/APPS are long-public; SFT data distilled from larger models that may have seen them.
Group-type evolution (Fig. 4) labelled by GPT-5.5 without validation.

coi.affiliations: USTC, Stanford University, Suzhou Institute for Advanced Research (USTC), Tongji University.
coi.funding: No acknowledgments or funding statement found.
coi.detail: Academic; only stake is the proposed method.

verdict_reason: Plausible RL credit-assignment idea with ablations and released code, but work-in-progress, single training seed, Python competitive programming only, abstract overstates gains, and it concerns model training rather than harness design.
applicability: Does not transfer to the Java team's harness decisions. The team uses hosted models via mixed agent hosts and will not run RL on coding policies; the tasks studied (single-file Python algorithm problems) say nothing about multi-repo the services or spec-driven workflows. At most, it is background on why vendor models may get better at multi-region edits.
